subject: Re: Tool/function calling integration patterns — next steps and architecture

Subject: Tool/function calling integration patterns — next steps

Hi Marissa,

Thanks again for the demo today — good overview of function calling and the routing options. A quick recap from our side and a few clarifying questions so we can align on an implementation path: 

- Primary use case: in-product assistant that can lookup accounts, surface transactions, and initiate payments via our internal services. Low-latency for conversational flows is important.
- We want structured, strongly-typed responses (JSON) to avoid brittle parsing on our side.
- Two major integration surfaces: (1) server-side calls from our backend (Node.js) and (2) a lightweight front-end companion for contextual suggestions (no direct secret usage in browser).
- Auth: we prefer short-lived service credentials; our security team prefers OAuth or ephemeral API keys and customer-managed KMS for secrets.
- Failover: plan to degrade gracefully (read-only responses or fallback to cached data) if downstream tools fail.

Open questions:
1) Recommended pattern for tool definitions (single combined tool vs. many fine-grained tools)?
2) Best practice for parallel tool calls when you need account + risk check + balance in one turn? Any guidelines on merging results and controlling latency?
3) SDK support for structured output + schema validation? Can you share a sample?

We also need a short architecture sketch and a sample that shows tool calling + parallel calls + error handling so our engineers can review. Can you send over an example and next steps?

Thanks,
James
Director of Product, FinApps

James — great meeting, thanks for the clear priorities. Attaching a short reference (redwood-tool-calling-reference.pdf) and a link to our repo with samples. High-level replies to your questions below, plus proposed next steps.

1) Tool definition granularity
- Start with fine-grained tools for orthogonal capabilities (account_lookup, transaction_query, payment_initiate, risk_check). Fine-grained tools give clearer failure domains and easier retries.
- Provide a composite orchestration layer (server-side) for complex flows that need transactional semantics. That layer can call multiple fine-grained tools and return a single structured response to the model.

2) Parallel calls and latency control
- For data that can be fetched in parallel (account metadata, balance, risk score), call tools in parallel from the orchestration service. Use configurable per-tool timeouts (e.g., 200–500ms) and a global deadline for the turn.
- If a tool times out, return a partial result plus a status field so the model or UI can surface "incomplete" data and optionally re-request.
- For low-latency paths, consider caching recent account lookups in Redis and using prefix/KV caching at the Redwood runtime to avoid repeated calls.

3) SDK + structured output
- Our SDKs support function/schema-based tool calling and JSON schema validation on responses. We can provide a Node.js example that registers tools with types and validators.

Proposed next steps
- Mateo will draft an architecture sketch showing front-end vs. server-side flows, auth options, and routing (hosted vs dedicated).
- Dev will propose auth patterns (ephemeral keys vs OAuth) and notes on Private deployment if you need VPC + KMS.
- We'll send a sample repo and a short walkthrough doc this week.

Action items: Mateo: architecture sketch (due Wed 11/11). Dev: auth options + shortlist (due Wed 11/11). Marissa: sample + reference (sent).

Best,
Marissa Cole
Account Executive, Redwood Inference

From: Mateo Alvarez <mateo_alvarez@redwood.ai>

Subject: Re: Tool/function calling integration patterns — next steps

James — adding some technical patterns that map to your questions. Happy to walk through on a short call.

High level architecture
- Front-end (no secrets): sends user context to a backend orchestration service. Backend holds secrets and calls Redwood API.
- Backend orchestration: translates model intent to tool calls; composes parallel calls; enforces timeouts/retries and transactional semantics where needed.
- Redwood runtime: hosts the model, manages batching, and routes to dedicated/private infra per policy. The model invokes tool definitions (function calls) that are proxied back to your orchestration API.

Tool definition patterns
- Define tool schema: name, input_schema (JSON Schema), output_schema, idempotency_key (optional), timeout_ms, retry_policy. Example names: account_lookup, txn_search, payment_initiate, risk_check, embeddings_search, reranker.
- Keep side-effecting tools (payment_initiate) behind an explicit confirmation step: model responds with a signed proposal object that the backend validates before executing.

Parallel tools & merging results
- Fan-out pattern: backend issues parallel HTTP calls for independent tools (account_lookup, risk_check, balance). Use Promise.all with per-call timeouts and a soft global deadline (e.g., 700ms).
- Merge policy: define a priority ordering and a merge function: successful results + partial indicators + error codes. Response to model: {data: {...}, statuses: {risk_check: "timeout"}}. 
- Use a short-circuit for critical calls: if risk_check fails and is required for payments, fail fast with a clear error path rather than returning stale data.

Embeddings + reranker pattern
- Use embeddings for semantic retrieval (customer docs, transaction notes). Return top-N candidate IDs to the model or a reranker.
- Reranker runs either (a) on the backend (preferred for consistency) or (b) as a model step where the model scores candidates given the query. If you run a model reranker, return its scores as part of the structured response so the UI can decide thresholds.

Error handling and idempotency
- Idempotency keys for side effects; explicit confirmation for irreversible actions.
- Retries: exponential backoff for transient 5xx, do not retry 4xx. Respect idempotency to avoid double charges.
- Circuit breaker: if downstream service error rate > threshold, return degraded mode to the model and mark tool as unavailable.

Sample snippets and repo
- The repo includes a Node.js server that registers tools with input/output schemas and demonstrates: parallel calls, timeouts, merging results, and a confirm+execute flow for payments. Link: https://github.com/redwood-inference/tool-calling-samples

I'll attach a simple architecture PNG in the next email.

— Mateo
Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference

Quick implementation notes from infra/security perspective:

Auth & secrets
- Ephemeral credentials: recommend short-lived JWTs issued by your auth service (rotate every 5–15 minutes) and use those for backend→Redwood calls or for orchestration service→downstream tools.
- For server-to-server, OAuth2 client_credentials with rotating secrets stored in your KMS is fine. For Private/VPC deployments, we can integrate with your KMS/HSM for key wrapping.

Routing & deployments
- If you expect sustained high throughput for the assistant, dedicated pools are best (predictable latency and throughput). For early-stage or low volume, hosted is cheaper. We can do mixed routing: user-tiered policy that routes FinApps production traffic to dedicated, dev/test to hosted.

Observability & retries
- Add per-tool metrics: latency, error rate, timeout count. Instrument merge logic so you can see which parallel call caused degradation.
- Timeouts: client-side per-call (200–500ms) and a global request deadline (700–1000ms) depending on UX SLAs.

Edge cases
- Partial responses: return explicit status codes in the structured output (OK, TIMEOUT, ERROR) and a human-friendly message for UI.
- Duplicate payments: require idempotency_key + backend double-check before executing; keep a write-ahead log to reconcile.

I'll include a short doc with code examples for JWT issuance and a sample nginx proxy config for routing to dedicated vs. hosted.

— Dev
